opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at MIT I didn't see myself as someone who would start a company. I was deep in math: taking graduate courses, doing research in number theory and combinatorics, thinking mostly about problems and proofs. Entrepreneurship felt like a different world. It was around me, of course. MIT has a very strong startup culture, and friends were building things, going to hackathons, talking about fundraising. But to me it seemed like something for people with a product idea or a business instinct, and I thought of myself as a researcher first.

Looking back, though, some of the ingredients were already there. What I loved about math research was taking on a problem that nobody knew how to solve, living with uncertainty for a long time, and slowly building the tools you need. That's not so different from starting a company. You're betting on something that isn't obvious yet, and you have to keep going when most signals say it might not work.

What changed for me came later, when I saw how quickly AI was progressing, especially in reasoning, and realized the intersection of mathematics and AI could be a real opportunity. It wasn't just a research question anymore. You needed a team, compute, and the ability to move fast, and a startup was the right vehicle. So at MIT entrepreneurship was something I admired from a bit of a distance. Only later did I realize it could be a natural continuation of what I cared about in math, not a departure from it.

r001.rationale: She says she saw herself as a researcher and viewed entrepreneurship from a distance, but does not state that becoming a professor was preferable to entrepreneurship.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I was at MIT I didn't think of myself as an entrepreneur at all. I was a math person. I'd spent years doing competition math, then research — Oxford, MIT, Stanford — and the people I admired were the ones proving theorems, not the ones raising rounds. If you'd told me at nineteen that I would start a company, I probably would have said that sounded like a distraction from the real work.

But MIT changes your relationship to that question, almost without you noticing. You're surrounded by people who treat building something as just another way of doing research. A friend would mention over dinner that they'd incorporated something, and it wasn't a big dramatic decision, it was closer to "I had an idea and I wanted to see if it was true." That reframing mattered to me. I started to see a company less as a business and more as an experiment with higher stakes and a faster feedback loop.

The other thing was watching what was happening with AI and mathematics. I had this slightly uncomfortable realization that the problems I cared about — formal reasoning, verification, whether machines could actually do mathematics rather than imitate it — were not going to be answered by one person writing papers. They needed teams, compute, engineers, and a kind of urgency that academia isn't really set up for. So entrepreneurship stopped being a career category I was choosing between and became more like the only vehicle that could carry the question I wanted to ask.

I'd say my view shifted from "entrepreneurship is for people who want to make money" to "entrepreneurship is what you do when the problem is bigger than you." That shift happened at MIT, even though I didn't act on it until later.

r001.rationale: She says she valued proving theorems and initially saw starting a company as a distraction, but does not state that she preferred becoming a professor.

astra-6.text: At MIT, I saw entrepreneurship as a way to turn an idea into something useful. You can have a beautiful technical solution, but building a company means asking another set of questions: Who needs this? What problem does it actually solve? And will people use it? That connection between intellectual curiosity and practical impact was what appealed to me.

r001.rationale: The response describes entrepreneurship as a way to turn ideas into practical impact, but does not say Carina Hong preferred becoming a professor.

sol-6.1.text: At MIT, entrepreneurship felt like a very natural extension of being curious and building things. You could start with a question—why does this work this way, or could we do it better?—and then try to turn that into something useful. What appealed to me was that you didn’t have to have everything figured out before you started. You could build something, learn from people’s reactions, and keep improving it.
